# True or false: Strategy

Most engineering waste starts here: goals with no diagnosis, tools chosen before problems, and work that never stops. See how well you can tell a real strategy from a wish list.

10 statements (Foundation 4, Standard 6). Decide whether each one is true or false before you open the answer. Every answer says why and links to the page that teaches it.

Prefer the terminal? From the repository root, run `python3 exercises/quiz.py --area strategy`.

### 1. A list of goals such as 'be cloud native, ship faster, improve quality' is a sound technical strategy.

Level: Foundation

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** Goals without a diagnosis give nobody a reason to rule anything in or out. A strategy starts by naming what is stopping you today, then sets a guiding policy and three to seven coherent actions. If you cannot write the diagnosis, collect evidence before setting goals.

Read more: [playbook/strategy/technical-strategy.md](../../playbook/strategy/technical-strategy.md)

</details>

### 2. A technical strategy should fit on one page and name no more than seven actions.

Level: Foundation

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**True.** The playbook asks for one page: a diagnosis, a guiding policy and three to seven actions. When fifteen actions are all marked high, nothing is a priority. Rank the actions and name what you will not do.

Read more: [playbook/strategy/technical-strategy.md](../../playbook/strategy/technical-strategy.md)

</details>

### 3. Doing what the large tech companies do is a safe starting point for most organisations' technical strategy.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** Their problems, scale and constraints are not yours, so their answers often do not fit. The playbook calls this a borrowed diagnosis. Start from your own evidence about what slows you down.

Read more: [playbook/strategy/technical-strategy.md](../../playbook/strategy/technical-strategy.md)

</details>

### 4. Building your own version of a commodity tool is usually cheaper than buying one, because there is no licence fee.

Level: Foundation

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** The licence fee is a small part of the cost; maintenance over five years is the large part, and a home-grown commodity tool rarely wins on it. Build only what differentiates you. Compare options on total cost of ownership over 3 to 5 years, including the cost of leaving.

Read more: [playbook/strategy/build-buy-adopt.md](../../playbook/strategy/build-buy-adopt.md)

</details>

### 5. In a weighted scoring matrix for a build or buy decision, the weights should be agreed before anyone scores the options.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**True.** Weights chosen after scoring can be bent to favour the option people already wanted. Agree and record the weights first, then score. This keeps the decision honest and defensible later.

Read more: [playbook/strategy/build-buy-adopt.md](../../playbook/strategy/build-buy-adopt.md)

</details>

### 6. In a business case, engineering hours saved can be counted as cash savings.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** Finance counts cash only when headcount or spend actually falls. Say what the saved hours will be used for instead. Show low, expected and high cases and commit to the low one.

Read more: [playbook/strategy/business-case.md](../../playbook/strategy/business-case.md)

</details>

### 7. A transition should include a pilot with an average team, not only with the strongest one.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**True.** A pilot that succeeds only with the best team tells you little about the other teams. The playbook adds a second pilot with an average team. That pilot shows the support and training the rest of the organisation will need.

Read more: [playbook/strategy/transition-playbook.md](../../playbook/strategy/transition-playbook.md)

</details>

### 8. At each gate of a transition programme, stopping is a planned and valid outcome.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**True.** Every gate chooses one of three outcomes: continue, change scope or stop. Funding one phase at a time keeps stopping cheap. Write the stop conditions in the charter and honour them, rather than treating stop as failure.

Read more: [playbook/strategy/transition-playbook.md](../../playbook/strategy/transition-playbook.md)

</details>

### 9. Planning 100% of engineering capacity for features is the most efficient use of a team.

Level: Foundation

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** Reliability, debt and platform work still happen; they just happen unplanned and invisible. The playbook sets an explicit capacity split for them. Planning to full capacity also leaves no room for the unplanned work that always arrives.

Read more: [playbook/strategy/portfolio-and-capacity.md](../../playbook/strategy/portfolio-and-capacity.md)

</details>

### 10. It is sensible to wait until regulators confirm final dates before preparing for new rules.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** Dates move, but the preparation is useful whatever the final date. The EU AI Act high-risk dates were moved by the 2026 Digital Omnibus, yet a register of AI use cases is needed either way. Start the cheap, no-regret work now, such as inventories and owners.

Read more: [playbook/strategy/horizon-scan.md](../../playbook/strategy/horizon-scan.md)

</details>
